_doc: Completed T-0484 ledger. Every frozen-manifest member received a dated repository/source-register review and targeted exact/variant-name sweep. Unlisted overrides use the documented no-corroboration default; pending is empty.
default_summary: No reliable record in the reviewed repository newspaper/reference corpus, Chicago directories, digitized county/local histories, institutional records and targeted exact/variant-name web sweep could be tied to this postal person with sufficient date/place/occupation/kinship discriminators. This is a documented no-corroboration result, not evidence that the person did not exist.
query_templates: justified OCR/spelling variants where the printed form was visibly suspect
search_scope: repository Chicago Democrat transcriptions, newspaper identity ledger and resident/source records
Fergus Chicago directories and existing resident-research source registry
Cook, Will, Kane, Lake and neighboring-county local histories
government, tribal, library and archival institutional records
broad exact-name and justified OCR/spelling-variant web searches

boilvin_nicholas.summary: The exact uncommon name Nicholas Boilvin appears in multiple 1834 Chicago post-office returns and independently in the 1833 Treaty of Chicago payment schedule. The paired contemporary-era evidence safely corroborates the identity and treaty-era Chicago/Cook County context; it does not by itself prove a July 1, 1835 dwelling.

vasseur_noel.summary: The exact uncommon name Noel Vasseur appears in the 1835 Chicago postal list and independently in the 1833 Treaty of Chicago payment schedule. This corroborates the identity and fur-trade/treaty-era regional context, while later Will/Kankakee geography means the letter must not be converted into a Chicago household claim.

barrows_mary.summary: Later early-Chicago education histories independently name Mary Barrows as Miss Chappel's associate/assistant and as a participant in the LaSalle Street boarding house for scholars. Combined with the exact postal-list name, this corroborates the Chicago educator identity without establishing a separate July 1, 1835 household.

cleland_martin.summary: An 1886 family genealogy gives an unusually specific migration chronology: Martin Cleland traveled from Chautauqua, New York, to Chicago on a prospecting tour in 1834 and selected a future home near Niles, Michigan; the family moved west in 1835. The uncommon exact name and matching Chicago year corroborate the postal person, but the Niles destination prevents a July 1835 Chicago-residence inference.

christy_nathan.summary: The 1834 Chicago letter-list evidence places Nathan Christy beside the uncommon Rumsey Christy, and the 1843 Chicago directory independently lists both Nathan Christy and Rumsey Christy. That paired-name continuity is a strong discriminator beyond a lone same-name match and corroborates Nathan's Chicago identity, while the later directory is not back-projected to a specific 1835 address or occupation.

elisha_rayond.summary: Racine County old-settler records identify Elisha Raymond Sr. traveling by vessel to Chicago and then Racine before settling the town of Raymond on September 22, 1835. 'Rayond Elisha' is a plausible transcription/order variant and the Chicago transit is striking, but it occurs after the July 1 scene date and no source bridges the postal spelling to this man.

candidates.basis: Rare name plus documented Chicago transit in 1835.
conflicts: The dated Chicago transit is September 1835, after the scene date; no direct bridge to the printed Rayond entry.

mclintock_thomas.summary: Cook County biography places Thomas McClintock Sr. and his son Thomas Franklin McClintock in Bachelor's Grove from fall 1833. This is strong family-level Cook County chronology, but two Thomas McClintocks are simultaneously available and the postal item cannot safely identify either one.

candidates.basis: Exact Thomas McClintock name within a Cook County family present from 1833.
conflicts: Both father and son are Thomas; no discriminator assigns the letter to either individual, and Bachelor's Grove is not Chicago proper.

hon_reynolds_john.summary: The honorific-bearing 'Reynolds John Hon.' could be former Illinois governor and sitting U.S. Representative John Reynolds. Government biography confirms his 1834-1837 congressional service, but his political/home geography was southwestern Illinois and Washington rather than a Chicago household.

candidates.basis: Honorific, exact name, and unique statewide prominence in the target period.
conflicts: Government biography supplies competing Belleville/congressional geography; a Chicago waiting letter alone cannot identify him.

moody_robert.summary: Kane County history lists Robert Moody among the first St. Charles-area settlers arriving in 1834. Exact name and target-period northeastern Illinois chronology make a useful regional candidate, but Fox River residence competes with bodily Chicago residence and no postal bridge is explicit.

candidates.basis: Exact name among first St. Charles-area settlers in 1834.
conflicts: Kane County/Fox River geography competes with Chicago; no independent bridge to the postal item.

hutchins_nathan.summary: Will County history places Nathan Hutchins under the bluff west of the Des Plaines in the early settlement period, with his father dying there in 1835 and the family moving toward Rockford in 1836. Exact name and target-period nearby geography are useful, but the source establishes a Will County household rather than a Chicago one.

candidates.basis: Exact name and documented Des Plaines/Will County residence in the target period.
conflicts: Competing Will County geography; no direct source ties the settler to the Chicago post-office entry.

hawley_oscar_l.summary: An Illinois Digital Archives 1842 Will County property roll indexes Oscar L. Hawley. The exact rare full name makes a useful later regional continuity lead, but the seven-to-eight-year gap and Will County geography prevent assertion.

candidates.basis: Rare exact full name in a later institutional Will County property record.
conflicts: 1842 is substantially later than the 1834 letter and no independent Chicago bridge exists.

bomgarten_moritz.summary: A Cook County genealogy index points to Moritz Baumgarten, stating that he came to Chicago with his family in 1836. The uncommon Bomgarten/Baumgarten spelling pair and later Chicago connection are compelling as a lead, but the stated 1836 arrival conflicts with treating him as the 1835 postal person without further evidence.

candidates.basis: Uncommon given name/surname variant plus later Chicago family biography.
conflicts: Indexed source states Chicago arrival in 1836, after the postal return; underlying volume/independent bridge is needed.

selden_saml_l.summary: Samuel L. Selden is independently documented by Rochester institutional records as living in Rochester and serving as first judge of Monroe County court from 1831 through 1837. The initials/name fit the postal entry but the exact-period New York chronology is strong competing geography, so identity is not asserted.

candidates.basis: Exact initials/name and a prominent contemporary person.
conflicts: Rochester judicial residence/service spans the target period; no evidence links that judge to the Chicago postal item.

titur_starr.summary: Lake County institutional history identifies Starr Titus as the county's first coroner, elected in 1839. 'Starr TituR' is a plausible OCR/transcription form of the rare Starr Titus name, but the evidence is four years later and supplies no direct Chicago postal bridge.

candidates.basis: Rare exact name (allowing final-letter OCR error) in northeastern Illinois by 1839.
conflicts: Four-year gap after the postal return; no direct evidence connects the Lake County official to the 1835 letter.
